subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a large frontal hemispheric mass develops worsening intracranial pressure. The cingulate gyrus is displaced beneath the falx cerebri. The clinical team anticipates the vascular and white-matter structures most likely to be compressed.
question: Which of the following neurologic deficits is most likely to result directly from this herniation?

options.text: Ipsilateral blown pupil from CN III compression
Contralateral lower extremity weakness from anterior cerebral artery compression
Duret hemorrhages from basilar artery branch rupture
Ipsilateral Horner syndrome from oculosympathetic pathway disruption
Contralateral facial weakness from middle cerebral artery compression

explanation_correct: Cingulate, or subfalcine, herniation occurs beneath the falx cerebri and can compress the anterior cerebral artery, producing contralateral lower extremity weakness. If the dominant hemisphere is affected, compression of the arcuate fasciculus can also cause aphasia. This is the classic deficit of subfalcine herniation.

explanation_incorrect.A: An ipsilateral blown pupil from CN III compression is a feature of uncal transtentorial herniation, not subfalcine herniation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Duret hemorrhages from rupture of paramedian basilar artery branches occur with central downward transtentorial herniation, not subfalcine herniation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Horner syndrome is not a typical direct consequence of subfalcine herniation; it reflects oculosympathetic pathway disruption in other settings.
explanation_incorrect.E: Contralateral facial weakness from middle cerebral artery compression is not the classic deficit of subfalcine herniation, which affects the anterior cerebral artery.

educationalObjective: Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery, causing contralateral lower extremity weakness and, in the dominant hemisphere, aphasia.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a mass lesion develops acute neurologic deterioration. Early on, there is an ipsilateral dilated fixed pupil with contralateral hemiparesis. Later, the pupillary finding appears on the opposite side and the hemiparesis becomes ipsilateral to the original mass, a misleading false-localizing pattern.
question: Which of the following best explains this sequence of findings?

options.text: Subfalcine herniation with anterior cerebral artery compression
Central transtentorial herniation with Duret hemorrhages
Tonsillar herniation with foramen magnum compression
Cingulate herniation with arcuate fasciculus compression
Uncal transtentorial herniation with Kernohan notch phenomenon

explanation_correct: The uncus is the medial temporal lobe. In uncal transtentorial herniation, early herniation compresses CN III, producing an ipsilateral blown pupil with contralateral hemiparesis. Late herniation produces coma and the Kernohan phenomenon, in which compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle and CN III against the Kernohan notch causes misleading ipsilateral hemiparesis with or without a contralateral blown pupil. This false-localizing sequence is characteristic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Subfalcine herniation causes contralateral lower extremity weakness from anterior cerebral artery compression, not a blown pupil or Kernohan phenomenon.
explanation_incorrect.B: Central transtentorial herniation causes caudal brainstem displacement, Duret hemorrhages, and is usually fatal, not the false-localizing Kernohan sequence.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tonsillar herniation is cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum causing brainstem compression and death, not CN III pupillary findings.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cingulate herniation relates to the arcuate fasciculus and anterior cerebral artery, not pupillary changes or the Kernohan notch.

educationalObjective: Uncal transtentorial herniation causes an early ipsilateral blown pupil and contralateral hemiparesis, progressing to coma and the false-localizing Kernohan phenomenon.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a large supratentorial mass develops progressive coma. Autopsy shows caudal displacement of the brainstem with rupture of paramedian branches of the basilar artery and hemorrhages within the pons.
question: Which of the following herniation syndromes is most consistent with these findings?

options.text: Central downward transtentorial herniation
Subfalcine herniation
Uncal transtentorial herniation
Tonsillar herniation
Transcalvarial herniation through a skull defect

explanation_correct: Central, or downward, transtentorial herniation involves caudal displacement of the brainstem. This ruptures paramedian branches of the basilar artery, producing Duret hemorrhages, and is usually fatal. The vignette of a supratentorial mass, progressive coma, and pontine hemorrhages from basilar branch rupture matches this syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.B: Subfalcine herniation is cingulate gyrus displacement under the falx causing anterior cerebral artery compression, not brainstem Duret hemorrhages.
explanation_incorrect.C: Uncal transtentorial herniation causes ipsilateral CN III compression and the Kernohan phenomenon, not the classic Duret hemorrhage description.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tonsillar herniation is downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum with brainstem compression, not downward brainstem displacement from a supratentorial mass.
explanation_incorrect.E: Transcalvarial herniation is extrusion of brain tissue through a skull defect and is not associated with Duret hemorrhages from basilar artery branches.

educationalObjective: Central downward transtentorial herniation causes fatal brainstem displacement with Duret hemorrhages from basilar artery branch rupture.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a posterior fossa mass develops sudden respiratory arrest. Imaging shows the cerebellar tonsils displaced through the foramen magnum with compression of the brainstem.
question: Which of the following best describes the most likely outcome of this herniation?

options.text: Contralateral lower extremity weakness from anterior cerebral artery compression
Ipsilateral blown pupil with contralateral hemiparesis
Coma and death from brainstem compression
Aphasia from arcuate fasciculus compression
False-localizing ipsilateral hemiparesis from the Kernohan notch

explanation_correct: Cerebellar tonsillar herniation occurs when the cerebellar tonsils herniate into the foramen magnum. These herniations compress the brainstem, and coma and death result. This is a neurosurgical emergency, consistent with the sudden respiratory arrest in this patient.

explanation_incorrect.A: Contralateral lower extremity weakness from anterior cerebral artery compression is a feature of subfalcine herniation, not tonsillar herniation.
explanation_incorrect.B: An ipsilateral blown pupil with contralateral hemiparesis is the early presentation of uncal transtentorial herniation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aphasia from arcuate fasciculus compression can occur with dominant hemisphere subfalcine herniation, not with tonsillar herniation.
explanation_incorrect.E: False-localizing hemiparesis from the Kernohan notch is a late uncal phenomenon, not a feature of tonsillar herniation.

educationalObjective: Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the brainstem, causing coma and death.
